questions.stem: Which of the following symbols of elements is derived from a Latin name?
explanation_steps: Most symbols come from the English name of the element (O = oxygen, C = carbon, Ca = calcium, Al = aluminium).

The textbook's table of symbols from Latin names includes sodium Na (natrium), potassium K (kalium), copper Cu (cuprum), silver Ag (argentum), gold Au (aurum), iron Fe (ferrum), tin Sn, antimony Sb, mercury Hg and lead Pb.
Na comes from 'natrium'. Answer: C.
tips: If the symbol does not match the English name (Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pb, Hg, Sn, Sb), it comes from Latin.

similar_questions.stem: The symbol of which element comes from its Latin name 'ferrum'?
explanation_steps: Ferrum → Fe = iron. Answer: B.

questions.stem: An ion of an atom has a net charge of +1, 18 electrons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is
explanation_steps: A +1 ion has one electron fewer than protons: protons = 18 + 1 = 19 (Z = 19, potassium).
Mass number = protons + neutrons = 19 + 18 = 37.
37 is not among the options. C (19) is the atomic number, not the mass number; E (39) is the mass number of the common isotope ³⁹K (19 p, 20 n), which is probably what the setter had in mind.
Correct value 37 – no option is right; E is keyed as the most likely intended answer (teacher decision).
tips: Cation: protons = electrons + charge. Anion: protons = electrons − charge. Then A = protons + neutrons.

similar_questions.stem: An ion with charge 2− has 18 electrons and 16 neutrons. Its mass number is
explanation_steps: Protons = 18 − 2 = 16 (sulphur); A = 16 + 16 = 32. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
textbook_ref.section: 2.1.1–2.1.3 The atom, subatomic particles, atomic and mass number

questions.review_flag: No correct option: a +1 ion with 18 electrons has 19 protons, so with 18 neutrons A = 37, which is not offered. E (39, i.e. ³⁹K with 20 neutrons) is keyed as the probable intent. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of matter?
explanation_steps: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
Gold (element), carbon monoxide (compound), steam (water vapour) and brass (alloy of Cu and Zn) all have mass and volume.
Heat is a form of energy – it has no mass and occupies no space. Answer: C.
tips: Energy forms (heat, light, sound, electricity) are not matter.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is matter?
explanation_steps: Air is a mixture of gases – it has mass and occupies space. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a colligative property of a solution?
explanation_steps: Colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, not on their identity: vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure.
Colour and solubility depend on the nature of the solute; partial and atmospheric pressure are properties of gases. Answer: D.
tips: Four colligative properties: ΔP (vapour pressure), ΔTb, ΔTf, osmotic pressure.

similar_questions.stem: Adding salt to water raises its boiling point. This is an example of

options.C: an intensive property of the solvent only

explanation_steps: Boiling-point elevation depends on the number of dissolved particles – a colligative property. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Dobereiner's triads?

options.A: Elements were arranged in the order of increasing atomic number.
options.B: Elements with similar properties were arranged into groups of eight.
options.C: Elements were arranged in the order of increasing atomic mass.
options.D: All the elements were classified properly.
options.E: No similarities were noticed among the known elements.

explanation_steps: Döbereiner (1829) placed elements with similar properties in groups of three (triads).
Within a triad, written in order of increasing atomic mass, the middle element's atomic mass is roughly the average of the other two (Li 6.9, Na 23, K 39).
Atomic number was not known then (A is wrong); groups of eight are Newlands' octaves (B); only a few triads were found (D wrong); the triads were based on similarities (E wrong). Answer: C.
tips: Döbereiner – triads (3); Newlands – octaves (8); Mendeleev – atomic mass table; Moseley – atomic number.

similar_questions.stem: In the triad Ca (40), Sr (?), Ba (137), the predicted atomic mass of Sr is about
explanation_steps: Average = (40 + 137)/2 = 88.5 (actual 87.6). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The correct name of the compound MgSO₄ is
explanation_steps: MgSO₄ contains Mg²⁺ and the polyatomic ion SO₄²⁻, which is sulphate.
Sulphide = S²⁻ (MgS); sulphite = SO₃²⁻ (MgSO₃). Prefixes such as 'tetra' are not used for ionic compounds. Answer: C.
tips: -ide = single element anion; -ate = more oxygen; -ite = one oxygen fewer.

similar_questions.stem: The formula of calcium sulphite is
explanation_steps: Sulphite = SO₃²⁻; Ca²⁺ + SO₃²⁻ → CaSO₃. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons in the 4th energy level of an atom is
explanation_steps: The maximum number of electrons in shell n is 2n².
For n = 4 (the N shell): 2 × 4² = 32. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: The maximum number of electrons that the M shell (n = 3) can hold is
explanation_steps: 2n² = 2 × 9 = 18. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The pH of a solution can be estimated with
explanation_steps: Acid–base indicators (litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein, universal indicator/pH paper) change colour over known pH ranges, so they estimate the pH.
A thermometer measures temperature, a barometer atmospheric pressure, a manometer gas pressure and a calorimeter heat. Answer: E.
tips: Estimate pH with indicators / pH paper; measure it accurately with a pH meter.

similar_questions.stem: A solution turns universal indicator red. Its pH is most likely
explanation_steps: Red on universal indicator = strongly acidic. Answer: A.

questions.stem: A 1 M solution of NaNO₃ and a 1 M solution of KCl have the same

options.A: mass of solute in 1 L of solution.
options.B: volume of solute in 1 L of solution.
options.C: percent by mass of solute in 1 L of solution.
options.D: number of moles of solute in 1 L of solution.

explanation_steps: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution, so 1 M means 1 mol of solute per litre for both solutions.
The molar masses differ (NaNO₃ 85 g/mol, KCl 74.5 g/mol), so the masses, mass percentages and densities differ. Answer: D.
tips: Equal molarity → equal moles per litre, not equal grams.

similar_questions.stem: How many moles of glucose are in 250 mL of a 2 M glucose solution?
explanation_steps: n = M × V = 2 mol/L × 0.250 L = 0.5 mol. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Group IA elements are also called
explanation_steps: Group IA (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) = alkali metals; IIA = alkaline earth metals; VIIA = halogens; VIIIA (0) = noble gases; B groups = transition elements. Answer: B.
tips: IA alkali, IIA alkaline earth, VIIA halogens, VIIIA noble gases.

similar_questions.stem: Chlorine, bromine and iodine belong to the
explanation_steps: They are group VIIA – the halogens. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The energy produced due to the motion of the particles of a substance is an example of
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Kinetic energy is energy due to the motion of the particles of a substance. The different forms of kinetic energy include thermal energy and electrical energy.'
Potential energy is due to position/composition (chemical, gravitational). The stem matches the textbook definition of kinetic energy. Answer: B.
Thermal energy (E) is itself a form of kinetic energy, but the general term defined this way is kinetic energy.
tips: Motion → kinetic (thermal, electrical); stored → potential (chemical, gravitational).

similar_questions.stem: Chemical energy stored in food is a form of
explanation_steps: Chemical energy is stored in bonds – potential energy. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following chemical substances is not an organic compound?
explanation_steps: Organic compounds are compounds of carbon, but a few carbon compounds – CO, CO₂ and carbonates such as CaCO₃ – are classed as inorganic.
Ethanol, acetic acid, benzene and methane are organic. Answer: B.
tips: Carbon oxides, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates and cyanides are inorganic.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an inorganic compound?
explanation_steps: CO₂ is one of the few inorganic carbon compounds. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1.1 Introduction – organic compounds are compounds of carbon

questions.stem: All of the following are properties of bases, except that they
explanation_steps: Bases neutralise acids, turn red litmus blue, feel slippery and taste bitter.
Turning blue litmus red is a property of ACIDS. Answer: C.
tips: Base → Blue litmus (both start with B).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a property of acids?
explanation_steps: Acids turn blue litmus red. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a method of base preparation?

options.A: The reaction of very active metals with water
options.B: Combination of a non-metal oxide and water
options.C: The reaction of a metal oxide with water
options.E: The reaction of potassium and water

explanation_steps: Textbook methods of preparing bases (G10 p.127): 1. very active metal + water (e.g. 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ – so A and E are methods); 2. metal oxide (basic anhydride) + water (C); 3. salt + base.
A non-metal oxide + water gives an ACID (SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄). Answer: B.
Note: 'direct combination of elements' (D) is also not a base method – the textbook lists it as a method for preparing ACIDS (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl), so D is also defensible.
tips: Non-metal oxides are acidic anhydrides; metal oxides are basic anhydrides.

similar_questions.stem: Which reaction produces a base?
explanation_steps: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; the others give acids. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 4.2.3 General methods of preparation of bases

additional_textbook_refs.section: 4.1.3 General methods of preparation of acids

questions.review_flag: Two options are not methods of preparing bases: B (non-metal oxide + water gives an acid, keyed) and D ('direct combination of elements' is listed in the textbook as a method for preparing ACIDS, p.121). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following bonding types is not an intramolecular attraction force?
explanation_steps: Intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) hold atoms together within a molecule or crystal: ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.
Intermolecular forces act between molecules: dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds.
Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force. Answer: D.
tips: 'Intra' = within (bonds); 'inter' = between (molecules).

similar_questions.stem: The forces that must be overcome when liquid water boils are mainly
explanation_steps: Boiling separates molecules; the O–H covalent bonds stay intact. Answer: C.

questions.stem: What is the percentage composition of oxygen (O) in hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)? [At. Mass: H = 1, O = 16]
explanation_steps: Formula mass of H₂O₂ = 2(1) + 2(16) = 34.
Mass of oxygen = 2 × 16 = 32.
Trap: 47.06 % (A) uses only one O atom (16/34); 5.88 % (D) is the percentage of hydrogen.
tips: Multiply the atomic mass by the number of atoms of that element in the formula.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of Argon (Ar) is [At. Number: Ar = 18]
explanation_steps: Fill 18 electrons in order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 18.
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. B has 17 electrons (Cl), C 20 (Ca), D 10 (Ne), E 12 (Mg). Answer: A.
tips: Add the superscripts – they must equal the atomic number (for a neutral atom).

similar_questions.stem: Which is the electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11)?

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about the particles in the solid state of matter? The particles
explanation_steps: In a solid the particles are packed closely in fixed positions with little space between them; they can only vibrate about those positions.
Particles that move freely describe a gas (and, to a lesser extent, a liquid). Answer: D.
tips: Solid: fixed shape and volume – particles vibrate only.

similar_questions.stem: In which state do particles have the greatest freedom of movement and the largest spaces between them?
explanation_steps: Gas particles are far apart and move randomly and freely. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The atoms of the isotopes of an element have the same number of

options.A: protons but differing numbers of neutrons.
options.B: neutrons but differing numbers of electrons.
options.C: electrons but differing numbers of protons.
options.D: neutrons but differing numbers of protons.
options.E: protons but differing numbers of electrons.

explanation_steps: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same atomic number = same number of protons) with different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons (e.g. ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C). Answer: A.
tips: Isotopes: same Z, different A.

similar_questions.stem: ¹⁶O, ¹⁷O and ¹⁸O differ in their number of
explanation_steps: All have 8 protons; neutrons are 8, 9 and 10. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The solid substance in which the atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in an orderly manner is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'A crystal or a crystalline solid is a solid substance in which the atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in an orderly, repeating' pattern.
The crystal lattice is the regularly spaced pattern (not the substance); the unit cell is the smallest repeating unit; an amorphous solid has no regular arrangement. Answer: B.
tips: Crystal = the solid; lattice = the pattern; unit cell = the repeating box.

similar_questions.stem: The smallest repeating unit from which a whole crystal can be built is the
explanation_steps: The unit cell is repeated in three dimensions to build the crystal. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds has the same molecular and empirical formula?
explanation_steps: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
C₆H₆ → CH; C₆H₁₂ → CH₂; C₂H₆ → CH₃; C₆H₁₂O₆ → CH₂O.
CH₄ cannot be simplified, so its empirical and molecular formulas are the same. Answer: E.
tips: If the subscripts share a common factor, divide it out to get the empirical formula.

similar_questions.stem: The empirical formula of C₄H₁₀ is
explanation_steps: Divide 4 and 10 by 2: C₂H₅. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following intermolecular forces exists between two adjacent HCl molecules?
explanation_steps: HCl is a polar molecule (Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻). The textbook: 'there is a small dipole-dipole force of attraction between adjacent HCl molecules.'
There are no ions in HCl gas; hydrogen bonds need H bonded to F, O or N. Dispersion forces exist between all molecules but the characteristic force for polar HCl is dipole–dipole. Answer: C.
tips: Polar molecule without H–F/O–N bonds → dipole–dipole.

similar_questions.stem: Which pair of molecules attract each other mainly by hydrogen bonding?
explanation_steps: N–H bonds allow hydrogen bonding between NH₃ molecules. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
textbook_ref.section: 2.3.2 van der Waals forces – dipole-dipole interactions

questions.stem: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds which contain
explanation_steps: Hydrocarbons (alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, aromatics) are compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. Answer: C.
tips: Hydro-carbon = hydrogen + carbon.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a hydrocarbon?
explanation_steps: Propane C₃H₈ contains only C and H. Answer: C.

questions.stem: According to the "like dissolves like" principle, which pair of substances is soluble in water?
explanation_steps: Water is polar, so polar and ionic substances dissolve in it; non-polar substances do not.
KCl (ionic) and ethanol (polar, hydrogen-bonds with water) are both soluble in water.
Benzene, oil, bromine and CCl₄ are non-polar (sugar is soluble but its partner in A and C is not; CO₂ is only slightly soluble and CCl₄ is insoluble). Answer: D.
tips: Polar/ionic dissolve in polar; non-polar dissolve in non-polar.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance dissolves best in hexane (non-polar)?
explanation_steps: Iodine is non-polar – like dissolves like. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.1 Solubility of solutes in liquids – like dissolves like

questions.stem: All of the following species are isoelectronic, except [At. Number: O = 8, F = 9, Ne = 10, Mg = 12, Ar = 18]
explanation_steps: Ar is the only species without 10 electrons. Answer: E.
tips: Anion: add the charge to Z; cation: subtract it.

similar_questions.stem: Which ion is isoelectronic with argon (Z = 18)?
explanation_steps: Cl⁻ = 17 + 1 = 18 electrons. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Periodic properties – ionic radius of isoelectronic ions

questions.stem: During photosynthesis

options.A: solar energy is changed to heat energy.
options.B: chemical energy is changed to potential energy.
options.C: electrical energy is changed to light and heat energies.
options.D: light energy is changed to chemical energy.
options.E: solar energy is changed to light energy.

explanation_steps: In photosynthesis green plants absorb sunlight and use it to make glucose from CO₂ and water: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
The light energy is stored as chemical energy in the glucose. Answer: D.
tips: Photosynthesis: light → chemical. Respiration/combustion: chemical → heat (and light).

similar_questions.stem: Burning of charcoal mainly converts

options.B: chemical energy to heat and light energy

explanation_steps: Combustion releases the stored chemical energy as heat and light. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a property of ammonia? It
explanation_steps: Textbook: ammonia is a colourless gas with a characteristic choking (pungent) smell, lighter than air and very soluble in water; its water solution is weakly alkaline and turns red litmus blue.
Ammonia is basic, not acidic. Answer: E.
tips: NH₃ is the common basic gas – it turns moist red litmus blue.

similar_questions.stem: Which test identifies ammonia gas?

options.A: It turns moist blue litmus red
options.B: It turns moist red litmus blue

explanation_steps: Ammonia is alkaline and turns red litmus blue (and gives white fumes with HCl). Answer: B.

questions.stem: A weak acid

options.B: contains the highest percentage of hydronium ion.
options.C: contains a higher concentration of ionized acid molecules.
options.D: contains the highest number of hydronium ion.

explanation_steps: A weak acid (e.g. acetic acid) ionises only slightly (partially) in water; most of its molecules remain un-ionised.
Complete dissociation and a high hydronium concentration describe strong acids. Answer: E.
tips: Strong = completely ionised; weak = slightly ionised (equilibrium ⇌).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a strong acid?
explanation_steps: HCl ionises completely in water. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Esterification is the reaction between
explanation_steps: An ester forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol (acid catalyst), eliminating water:
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (ethyl ethanoate). Answer: B.
tips: Acid + alcohol → ester + water (esters smell fruity).

similar_questions.stem: The ester formed from ethanoic acid and methanol is
explanation_steps: Alkyl part from the alcohol (methyl), acid part becomes -oate (ethanoate). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of an exothermic reaction?
explanation_steps: Exothermic processes release heat: burning wood, combustion, freezing and condensation (both give out latent heat).
Photosynthesis absorbs light energy – it is endothermic. Answer: A.
tips: Changes that go to a more ordered state (gas → liquid → solid) release heat.

similar_questions.stem: Which process is endothermic?
explanation_steps: Melting absorbs heat from the surroundings. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs contains a weak base and a weak acid?
explanation_steps: Ammonia (NH₃) is a weak base; acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is a weak acid.
NaOH and KOH are strong bases; HCl, HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ are strong acids. Answer: B.
tips: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄. Strong bases: group IA hydroxides (and Ca, Sr, Ba).

similar_questions.stem: Which pair contains a strong acid and a strong base?
explanation_steps: HCl and NaOH are both completely ionised. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The solubility of gases in water

options.A: increases with increased temperature and pressure.
options.B: decreases with decreased temperature and pressure.
options.C: decreases with decreased temperature and increased pressure.
options.D: increases with decreased temperature and increased pressure.
options.E: increases with decreased temperature and pressure.

explanation_steps: Dissolving a gas is exothermic, so lowering the temperature increases gas solubility (cold water holds more O₂).
Henry's law: gas solubility increases with the pressure of the gas above the liquid (carbonated drinks are bottled under pressure).
So solubility increases with decreased temperature and increased pressure. Answer: D.
tips: Cold and high pressure = more dissolved gas; opening a warm soda releases CO₂.

similar_questions.stem: Why do bubbles form when a bottle of soda is opened?

options.B: The pressure above the liquid falls, so CO₂ becomes less soluble

explanation_steps: Lower pressure → lower gas solubility → CO₂ escapes. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.2 Effect of temperature and pressure on solubility

questions.stem: The most common form of energy transformation in chemical reactions is in the form of
explanation_steps: Chemical reactions may release or absorb light, electrical or heat energy, but by far the most common form of energy change is heat (exothermic and endothermic reactions). Answer: C.
tips: Energy change in a reaction is usually measured as heat, ΔH.

similar_questions.stem: The energy change of a reaction measured at constant pressure is called
explanation_steps: Heat exchanged at constant pressure = ΔH. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The hydrogen atomic bomb is based on
explanation_steps: The hydrogen bomb releases energy by fusing light hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium) into helium – nuclear fusion (a fission bomb is used only as the trigger).
The ordinary atomic bomb (uranium-235/plutonium) is based on fission. Answer: E.
tips: A-bomb = fission; H-bomb and the Sun = fusion.

similar_questions.stem: The energy of the Sun comes from

options.B: fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium

explanation_steps: Stars shine by nuclear fusion. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The bond angle in a tetrahedral electron pair arrangement is
explanation_steps: Four electron pairs around a central atom point to the corners of a tetrahedron to minimise repulsion; the angle between them is 109.5° (e.g. CH₄). Answer: D.
tips: 2 pairs linear 180°; 3 pairs trigonal planar 120°; 4 pairs tetrahedral 109.5°.

similar_questions.stem: The bond angle in BF₃ (three bonding pairs, no lone pair) is
explanation_steps: Trigonal planar arrangement → 120°. Answer: D.

questions.stem: A reaction in which one element replaces a less active element from a solution of a compound is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'A reaction in which one element replaces a less active element in a compound is called a single replacement reaction', e.g. Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Answer: E.
tips: A + BC → AC + B (single); AB + CD → AD + CB (double).

similar_questions.stem: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu is an example of
explanation_steps: The more active iron replaces copper. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The temperature at which a pure substance changes from a solid to a liquid is called
explanation_steps: Melting point = temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid (for a pure substance it is sharp and constant).
Freezing point is liquid → solid (same temperature, opposite direction); boiling point liquid → gas; sublimation solid → gas. Answer: C.
tips: Melting: s → l; freezing: l → s; boiling: l → g; condensation: g → l; sublimation: s → g.

similar_questions.stem: The change of a gas directly into a solid is called
explanation_steps: Gas → solid is deposition (the reverse of sublimation). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following pair of atoms has the same number of valence electrons? [At. Number: N = 7, Na = 11, Mg = 12, K = 19]
explanation_steps: Configurations: N 2,5 (5 valence e⁻); Na 2,8,1 (1); Mg 2,8,2 (2); K 2,8,8,1 (1).
Na and K both have 1 valence electron – both are group IA. Answer: C.
tips: Same group = same number of valence electrons.

similar_questions.stem: Which element has the same number of valence electrons as oxygen (Z = 8)?
explanation_steps: O 2,6 and S 2,8,6 – both group VIA. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about an acid? An acid

options.B: produces a hydroxide ion in an aqueous solution.
options.E: liberates a hydroxide ion when it reacts with water.

explanation_steps: The word acid comes from Latin 'acidus' = sour; acids (lemon juice, vinegar) taste sour.
Acids produce H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions in water and donate protons; producing or donating OH⁻ and a bitter taste are properties of bases. Answer: D.
tips: Acid: sour, H⁺ donor. Base: bitter, OH⁻ producer / H⁺ acceptor.

similar_questions.stem: According to Arrhenius, a base is a substance that
explanation_steps: Arrhenius base = OH⁻ producer in aqueous solution. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In a cubic unit cell, the angle between each of the axes is
explanation_steps: Crystal systems are described by the edge lengths a, b, c and the axial angles α, β, γ of the unit cell.
Cubic: a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90°. Answer: B.
120° appears only in the hexagonal system (γ = 120°).
tips: Cubic: all edges equal, all angles 90°; tetragonal: a = b ≠ c, all 90°; orthorhombic: a ≠ b ≠ c, all 90°.

similar_questions.stem: A unit cell has a = b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90°. Its crystal system is
explanation_steps: Two equal edges, all right angles = tetragonal. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions represents an oxidation reaction?
explanation_steps: Oxidation = addition of oxygen (or loss of electrons / increase in oxidation number).
In C, sulphur gains oxygen and its oxidation number rises from 0 to +4 – sulphur is oxidised.

D and E show gain of electrons (reduction). In A sulphur gains hydrogen (0 → −2, reduced) and in B chlorine gains hydrogen (reduced) – each is a whole redox reaction rather than an 'oxidation' of the named non-metal. Answer: C.
tips: Gain of O or loss of H = oxidation; gain of H or gain of electrons = reduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following synthetic polymers is made by condensation polymerization?
explanation_steps: Wool, cotton, silk and starch are natural polymers, not synthetic.
Nylon is a synthetic polymer made by condensation polymerisation of a diacid (adipic acid) and a diamine (1,6-diaminohexane), eliminating water. Answer: D.
tips: Condensation polymers: nylon, polyester (lose H₂O). Addition polymers: polyethene, PVC, polystyrene.

explanation_steps: Coating iron or steel with zinc (by dipping in molten zinc) is galvanisation. Zinc is more active than iron, so it protects the iron even when scratched (sacrificial protection) – the corrugated iron sheets used for roofs are galvanised.

questions.stem: When the temperature of a gas increases within a closed container, pressure increases because

options.A: the frequency of collisions between molecules and the container walls decreases.
options.B: the frequency of collisions between molecules and the container walls increases.
options.C: the spaces between the molecules of gas decrease.

options.A: the amount of solvent that will dissolve in a given amount of a solute at any temperature.
options.B: the amount of solute that will dissolve in a given amount of solvent at any temperature.

questions.stem: One of the following cations has the highest tendency of gaining electrons.
explanation_steps: Gaining electrons = being reduced to the metal. The less active the metal, the more easily its cation is reduced (electrochemical series).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the energy diagram? (Diagram: enthalpy (0–1000) against reaction progress. The reactants A₂(g) + X₂(g) start at 650; the curve rises to a peak at about 950 and falls to the products 2AX(g) at 100.)
questions.image_alt: Enthalpy diagram on a grid: vertical axis 'Enthalpy' from 0 to 1000 in steps of 100, horizontal axis 'Reaction Progress'. A flat line labelled A₂(g) + X₂(g) at 650 rises in a hump to a maximum at about 950, then falls steeply to a flat line labelled 2AX(g) at about 100.

options.A: The reaction is exothermic with ΔH = −300 kJ.
options.B: The reaction is endothermic with ΔH = 850 kJ.
options.C: The reaction is exothermic with ΔH = 550 kJ.
options.D: The reaction is exothermic with ΔH = −850 kJ.
options.E: The reaction is exothermic with ΔH = −550 kJ.

explanation_steps: Read the graph: H(reactants, A₂ + X₂) ≈ 650 kJ; H(products, 2AX) ≈ 100 kJ; peak ≈ 950 kJ.
ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 100 − 650 = −550 kJ.
Products are lower than reactants, so heat is released – exothermic with ΔH = −550 kJ. Answer: E.
Traps: 300 kJ (A) is the activation energy (950 − 650); +550 (C) has the wrong sign for an exothermic reaction; 850 (B, D) is peak − products.
tips: Exothermic ⇔ products below reactants ⇔ ΔH negative.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct when a solute dissolves in a solvent?

options.A: The solute-solute attractions are greater than the solvent-solvent attractions.
options.B: The solute-solute attractions are less than the solvent-solvent attractions.
options.C: The solute-solvent attraction is greater than the sum of the solute-solute and solvent-solvent attraction.
options.D: There is a strong attraction between solute and solvent molecules.
options.E: The solvent-solvent attraction is greater than the sum of the solute-solute and solvent-solvent attraction.

explanation_steps: To dissolve, solute particles must be separated (breaking solute–solute attractions) and solvent molecules pushed apart (breaking solvent–solvent attractions); new solute–solvent attractions then form and release energy.
Dissolving is favoured when the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to overcome both – the setter's intended statement is C (and when they are larger the dissolution is exothermic).
D ('a strong attraction between solute and solvent') expresses the same idea less precisely and is also acceptable; A, B compare the wrong forces and E is self-contradictory. Answer: C.
tips: Like dissolves like: similar intermolecular forces make strong solute–solvent attractions possible.

options.A: endothermic – solute–solvent attractions are weaker than those broken
options.B: exothermic – solute–solvent attractions release more energy than was needed to separate the particles
options.C: a physical change with no energy change

explanation_steps: Warming means net heat release: energy of new attractions > energy to break old ones. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true?

options.A: Na and H have similar properties.
options.B: S²⁻ has smaller ionic radius than Cl⁻.
options.C: Ionization energy of an atom is influenced by nuclear charge.
options.D: Si and P have different properties.
options.E: F⁻ and Cl⁻ ions have similar chemical properties.

explanation_steps: S²⁻ and Cl⁻ are isoelectronic (18 electrons); S has 16 protons and Cl has 17, so the S²⁻ electron cloud is held less tightly and S²⁻ is LARGER (textbook Table 1.12: S²⁻ 1.84 Å; Cl⁻ 1.81 Å). B is false.
C is true (greater nuclear charge → higher ionisation energy); D is true (Si and P are in different groups); E is true (both are halide ions of group VIIA).

A is questionable: H and Na both have one valence electron and form +1 ions (that is why H is placed in group IA), but hydrogen is a non-metallic gas, so their properties are largely different. B is the clearly false statement. Answer: B.
tips: Isoelectronic ions: the fewer the protons, the bigger the ion (S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺).

similar_questions.stem: Which ion is the largest?
explanation_steps: All have 10 electrons; O²⁻ has the fewest protons (8). Answer: D.

questions.review_flag: Two statements are arguably untrue: B (S²⁻ is larger than Cl⁻ – keyed) and A ('Na and H have similar properties' – H is a non-metal gas, though both have one valence electron). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

options.C: ΔH is negative and the reaction is endothermic.

Answer questions 1.1 to 1.5 based on the following diagram. (5 points)
Hint: C and D are layers of water and oil.
(Diagram: a pear-shaped glass funnel held in a stand. B labels the stopper at the top; C labels the upper liquid layer; D labels the lower liquid layer; E labels the tap at the bottom.)
1.1 The name of the apparatus is ______.
1.2 The part of the apparatus used for closing while shaking the mixture is labelled by ___ and is called ______.

questions.image_alt: Separating funnel clamped beside a vertical stand rod. Label lines: B points to the round glass stopper at the top; C to the dark upper liquid layer; D to the lighter lower liquid layer in the cone; E to the tap (stopcock) at the bottom above the stem.
questions.answer: 1.1 Separating funnel; 1.2 B – stopper; 1.3 E – tap (stopcock); 1.4 C is the oil layer; 1.5 D is the water layer.

subparts.question: Part for closing while shaking (label and name)
steps: Closes the top of the funnel.

subparts.question: Part that allows separation (label and name)
steps: Opened to let the lower layer run out.

subparts.question: C is the ___ layer
steps: Oil is less dense – top layer.

explanation_steps: A separating funnel separates immiscible liquids such as oil and water (textbook Activity 1.15, Fig. 1.13).
The stopper (B) closes the top while the mixture is shaken; the tap or stopcock (E) at the bottom is opened to run off the lower layer.
Oil is less dense than water and does not mix with it, so oil floats as the upper layer (C) and water forms the lower layer (D).
marking_points: 1 point each: separating funnel; B = stopper; E = tap/stopcock; C = oil; D = water
1.2 and 1.3: both label and name needed for the full point (½ each)
tips: The denser liquid is always the lower layer; open the stopper before opening the tap so the liquid runs out smoothly.

questions.stem:
Given the equilibrium reaction below, indicate the effect of the following changes based on Le Chatelier's principle. (2 points)
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
3.1 Increase in pressure – shifts the equilibrium toward ______
3.2 Increase in volume – shifts the equilibrium toward ______
questions.answer: 3.1 Toward the right (products, NH₃ – fewer gas molecules). 3.2 Toward the left (reactants, N₂ and H₂ – more gas molecules).

subparts.question: Increase in pressure
steps: Fewer moles of gas on the right (2 < 4).

subparts.question: Increase in volume
steps: More moles of gas on the left.

explanation_steps: Le Chatelier: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change imposed on it.
Left side: 1 + 3 = 4 mol of gas; right side: 2 mol of gas.
Increasing the pressure is opposed by reducing the number of gas molecules → shift to the right (more NH₃).
Increasing the volume lowers the pressure; the system opposes this by making more gas molecules → shift to the left (reactants).
marking_points: 1 point each: 3.1 right/forward/toward NH₃; 3.2 left/backward/toward N₂ and H₂
tips: Pressure ↑ / volume ↓ → side with fewer gas moles; pressure ↓ / volume ↑ → side with more gas moles.

similar_questions.stem: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), which way does the equilibrium shift when (a) pressure is decreased, (b) SO₃ is removed?
similar_questions.answer: (a) To the left (3 mol gas side); (b) to the right (to replace SO₃).
explanation_steps: 3 mol gas ⇌ 2 mol gas; removing a product pulls the equilibrium toward the products.

6.1 In a cold morning at −13 °C, the air pressure in an automobile tire is 1.5 atm at a fixed volume. Calculate the pressure after the tire warmed to 15 °C. (2 points)
6.2 For a given amount of a gas, the relationship between (2 points)
a) pressure and temperature at constant volume is ______ proportional.
b) volume and temperature at constant pressure is ______ proportional.
questions.answer: 6.1 P₂ = 1.5 atm × 288 K / 260 K = 1.66 atm. 6.2 a) directly; b) directly.

subparts.label: 6.2a
subparts.question: P and T at constant V

subparts.label: 6.2b
subparts.question: V and T at constant P

explanation_steps: 6.1: At constant volume (Gay-Lussac's law) P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂, with temperatures in kelvin.
P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 1.5 atm × 288/260 = 1.66 atm (pressure rises as the air warms).
6.2 a) At constant volume P ∝ T (kelvin) – directly proportional (Gay-Lussac). b) At constant pressure V ∝ T – directly proportional (Charles's law).
marking_points: 6.1: 1 point for converting to kelvin and using P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂; 1 point for 1.66 atm (accept 1.65–1.7 atm)
No credit for an answer using °C (1.5 × 15/−13)
tips: Never put °C into a gas law – always convert to kelvin first. Only Boyle's law (P–V) is an inverse proportion.

Compare and contrast inorganic and organic compounds based on the given properties under the first column. (4 points)
Property | Inorganic compounds | Organic compounds
Usually the type of bond is | 7.1 | 7.5
Melting point | 7.2 | 7.6
Solubility in water | 7.3 | 7.7
Usually the particles are | 7.4 | 7.8
questions.answer: Inorganic: 7.1 ionic; 7.2 high; 7.3 (usually) soluble in water; 7.4 ions. Organic: 7.5 covalent; 7.6 low; 7.7 (generally) insoluble in water (soluble in non-polar solvents); 7.8 molecules.

subparts.question: Inorganic – melting point
steps: Mostly solids with high melting points.

subparts.question: Inorganic – solubility in water
steps: Water soluble, insoluble in non-polar solvents.

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.2 compares the two classes:
Type of bond: many inorganic compounds are ionic; organic compounds are mostly covalent.
Melting point: inorganic compounds are mostly solids with high melting points; organic compounds are gases, liquids or low-melting solids.
Solubility: inorganic compounds are generally water-soluble but insoluble in non-polar solvents; organic compounds are generally insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents.
Particles: inorganic – ions; organic – molecules.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct cell (8 cells × ½ = 4 points)
tips: Think of NaCl (ionic, high m.p., dissolves in water) versus wax (covalent molecules, low m.p., insoluble in water).

similar_questions.answer: Reactions: inorganic generally fast, organic generally slow. Electrical conductivity: inorganic conduct when molten or dissolved; organic generally do not conduct.
